The [NASA Technical Reports Server][ref_ntrs] and the [NASA History Office][ref_nasa_x3_factsheet] hold the record, and the [Armstrong Flight Research Center][ref_nasa_armstrong] is the institutional successor.

**The research survey holds 5,371 research records drawn from Crossref, the NASA Technical Reports Server and the Defense Technical Information Center**, of which 1,152 are report primaries, being 21.4 percent, by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary. **The median publication year is 1996.** Of the 5,295 dated records, 726 were published before 1960, the period in which the aircraft was designed and flown, being 13.7 percent, and 1,375 were published in 2015 or later, being 26.0 percent.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is on the NASA Technical Reports Server or it carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. **The NACA reports that carry this article's argument are report primaries under that rule**, and so are all of the X-3's own reports. **The rule does not reach the journal papers among the foundational sources**, such as Glauert on compressibility, Sears on minimum wave drag and Sutherland on viscosity, so 21.4 percent is a lower bound on how much of the survey is first-hand.

### Thin Subjects

**Six subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space. Where a row joins two groups of terms with the word together, a title must carry a term from each group.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the boundary layer diverter of a side inlet | diverter, diverters, diverterless, diverter less | 14 |
| the recovery temperature of a heated surface | recovery temperature, recovery factor, recovery factors, adiabatic wall temperature | 19 |
| springback of formed titanium sheet | springback together with titanium, Ti 6Al 4V, Ti6Al4V, TC4 | 13 |
| swing and pendulum measurement of inertia | swing, pendulum, bifilar, trifilar together with moment of inertia, moments of inertia | 25 |
| the mass distribution and inertia ratio of an airframe | mass distribution, inertia ratio, inertia distribution, radius of gyration, radii of gyration | 10 |
| engine and airframe development schedules | engine development, engine program, engine programme, engine delay, engine availability, engine substitution, engine selection | 8 |

**The diverter is a part the literature mostly sets out to remove.** Of the 14 titles, 8 describe diverterless inlets, and the side-inlet diverter of the X-3's own period appears in one NACA report on a diverter-type boundary-layer removal system for a scoop inlet at Mach 1.90.

**The recovery temperature is settled rather than neglected.** The relation that decides whether titanium was needed at Mach 2 is standard and tabulated, and a small literature of recovery factor measurements is the shape a settled subject takes.

**Springback of titanium is a small part of a large literature.** Titanium appears in 13 of the 274 titles that name springback, so the statement that titanium's elastic recovery after forming is roughly twice aluminium's rests on the yield-to-modulus relation derived above rather than on a body of titanium-specific measurement.

**The inertia of a whole aircraft is rarely the subject of a title.** Of the 25 titles on swing and pendulum methods, 2 name an aircraft or an unmanned air vehicle, and the rest are general metrology of moments of inertia. The coupling analysis depends on inertia entirely.

**Mass distribution was studied as a spin problem before it was a coupling problem.** Of the 10 titles that name mass distribution or an inertia ratio, 7 concern spinning or tumbling.

**The procurement lesson has almost no literature.** Eight titles name engine development, and none names a schedule, a delay or a substitution, so the conclusion that engine and airframe cannot be procured on independent schedules stands on the X-3's own history rather than on a published analysis.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject.** Many words this subject depends on also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded. Titanium is also a word of dentistry, orthopaedic implants and photocatalysis, and flutter is also a disorder of the heart. Fighter also names freedom fighters, fire fighters, video games and a lettuce cultivar, and Starfighter also names a film. Inertial coupling also belongs to two-phase flow, rotordynamics and satellite attitude, roll damping and roll coupling also belong to ships, barges and offshore platforms, and kinematic coupling is a fixture of precision engineering. Departure also names a flight leaving its gate, so air traffic scheduling is excluded. An afterburner is also a stage of a particle accelerator and a utility for graphics cards, an inlet is also a feature of a coastline and the mouth of a pipe, and the supersonic nozzle of a natural gas separator shares the inlet's gas dynamics and none of its subject. The wind tunnel also tests cars, trains, bridges, buildings and birds, and the pendulum measurement of a moment of inertia also serves sports equipment and internal-friction apparatus. Correction, withdrawal and erratum notices, trade news, parts catalogue listings, fastener and material specifications, bibliographies, and records that are parts of works rather than works, such as figure, table and front-matter records, are excluded as well, because a survey counts research works, and course and classroom material is excluded because a teaching exercise is not a method for an aircraft. Three families of titles that a shared exclusion list refuses elsewhere are admitted here because they are this subject, namely inlet buzz, the fracture of titanium alloys and the supersonic aerodynamics of missiles.

**A record whose only link to this subject is aeronautics in general is excluded too**, and so is one whose subject belongs to a class of vehicle the argument never uses. Rotorcraft, vertical and short takeoff aircraft, airships, small unmanned and micro air vehicles, airliners and light aircraft, spacecraft and launch vehicles are such classes, and so are aircraft and jet noise with the sonic boom, small and micro turbojets, fans, propellers and turboprops, titanium powder moulding and coatings, and flight control design methods the argument does not use. A method or phenomenon the argument relies on is admitted whatever the vehicle, so a study of flutter, loss of control, system identification or inertia measurement on another class of aircraft is kept, and so are the oblique-wing aircraft whose deliberate asymmetry makes coupling a design variable. A book chapter is a work and is judged by its subject. A review of a book, a dictionary or short reference entry, an editorial or news notice, and a second deposit of a document already counted, such as a conference copy of a report, are not research works and are not admitted. A signed comment on a paper, a discussion of it and its author's closure or reply are research works, because each argues about a result, and are admitted when their subject is.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Springback studies of steel and aluminium sheet are kept, because the springback relation this article derives for titanium is the same relation. General pendulum methods for measuring moments of inertia are kept, because the swing test is one of them. Recommended practices and design requirements for landing gear, wheels, tires and brakes, and titanium metallurgy that names no aircraft, share the subject's hardware or materials, and a reader may weigh each accordingly.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only.

## Epistemic State

Established historical fact includes the 1949 approval of construction, the single airframe and its serial, the substitution of Westinghouse J34 engines for the intended J46, the wing thickness ratio and aspect ratio, the extensive use of titanium, the first flight on 20 October 1952, the maximum speed of Mach 1.208 in a dive on 28 July 1953, the 51 flights, the coupling events flown by Joe Walker on 27 October 1954, and the aircraft's retirement in 1956 and preservation. These are documented in the sources cited.

Established engineering analysis includes every relation in the sizing sections. The thrust-limited Mach relation, the normal-shock recovery relation, the Ackeret result, the Bredt torsion relation, the divergence and reversal expressions, the takeoff relations, and the coupling threshold are standard results. The worked numbers are the author's own arithmetic applied to published inputs and are labelled as derived.

Inference includes the attribution of the performance shortfall to thrust and inlet losses in the proportions given. The thrust shortfall is documented and the normal-shock recovery is arithmetic, but the assignment of the residual between drag underestimate and installed-thrust shortfall is an interpretation the record does not settle. The claim that a fixed inlet was the second failure is an inference, because the sources consulted describe no variable geometry but do not describe the inlets at all, and the numerical split is weaker still.

Weakly supported are the representative values where the sources give no figures. The stiffness coefficients, the maximum lift coefficient, the ground friction and drag during the takeoff roll, and the assumed drag coefficients are plausible for an aircraft of this class rather than measured properties of this airframe. The moments of inertia are those tabulated by [Day 1997][research_coupling_history_1997], and the inertias the NACA used for this aircraft were the manufacturer's estimates according to [Fischel et al. 1957][research_x3_handling_1957]. The critical roll rate of 84 degrees per second rests on the assumed stiffness coefficients and should be read as establishing that the threshold lay within the aircraft's roll authority, not as a number this aircraft carried. [Day 1997][research_coupling_history_1997] reports a calculated critical roll velocity of 2.5 radians per second at the Mach 1.05 condition. The comparison with the X-2 figure of 255 uses the same method and the inertias Day tabulates for both aircraft, but both figures rest on the same assumed stiffness coefficients, so the ratio is indicative only.

Contested or unresolved in the sources consulted is the exact division of responsibility for the performance shortfall, the degree to which the titanium experience influenced later programmes, and the precise flight count, which is usually given as 51 but is stated without a counting rule. The inadvertent hop during the taxi test five days before the official first flight is variously counted and not counted. The sources also disagree on the Mach number of Walker's second roll, given as 1.05 by [Day 1997][research_coupling_history_1997] and as 1.154 by [Dinius 2014][ref_nasa_x3_stiletto].

A note on temporal position. This article carries an editorial date of 2025-10-09 and is written from current knowledge, including contemporary literature published well after that date.

## Conclusion

The Douglas X-3 was designed correctly against a specification that changed under it. Two engines producing seventy percent of the intended thrust, feeding through fixed inlets that lose a further twenty-eight percent of total pressure at the design Mach number, halve the thrust available. Halving thrust costs thirty percent of maximum Mach number, which takes a design value of 2.0 to about 1.42, and the aircraft managed 1.21. The keystone question, which is how a very thin very low aspect ratio wing behaves in sustained supersonic flight, was never asked of it.

What the aircraft did instead was reveal the consequence of its shape. A twenty-metre fuselage with a seven-metre wing has a pitch to roll inertia ratio near fifteen, about three times the [X-2][related_post_a299_bell_x2] value, and that puts the critical roll rate at about eighty-four degrees per second. That is a moderate control input. Joe Walker made an abrupt roll in October 1954, the aircraft departed violently in all three axes, and he recovered and did it again \[[Dinius 2014][ref_nasa_x3_stiletto]\]. The resulting data set arrived while a fighter fleet was losing aircraft to the same phenomenon and two years before it killed a pilot in the X-2 \[[Day 1997][research_coupling_history_1997]\].

The X-3 therefore fails its keystone completely and matters anyway. No sharper demonstration is available that design intent and historical contribution are different quantities. It also supplied a wing planform to the [F-104][ref_f104] and data for better tires, which is a more conventional kind of success and a smaller one.

The next article takes the [Northrop X-4 Bantam][ref_northrop_x4], a semi-tailless aircraft built to test whether the horizontal tail could be dispensed with at transonic speed, and which answered that question in the negative clearly enough that nobody asked it again for thirty years.
